implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines provides Channel as a first-class primitive: it is conceptually a BlockingQueue but with suspending send/receive instead of blocking ones, so a coroutine suspends rather than occupying a thread. The capacity is the design decision and it is a type-level constant: RENDEZVOUS (capacity 0, a pure rendezvous), CONFLATED (keeps only the latest - drop-oldest), BUFFERED (default 64), or UNLIMITED (never suspends the sender, which removes backpressure). Channel(capacity, onBufferOverflow) with BufferOverflow.SUSPEND / DROP_OLDEST / DROP_LATEST makes the full-behaviour explicit. close() is the producer's job; a receive on a closed-and-drained channel throws ClosedReceiveChannelException. onUndeliveredElement is the important safety feature: it is called for an element that was sent but not delivered (dropped, cancelled, or the receiver cancelled after taking), which is how a resource is closed rather than leaked. select { } on a channel suspends until one of several clauses is ready.
idiom_name: kotlinx.coroutines Channel (suspending send/receive) with capacity constants, BufferOverflow, close, and select
pitfalls: You must close() the channel (the producer's job) or every receive suspends forever; a receive on a closed-and-drained channel throws ClosedReceiveChannelException, which must be caught.
Channel.UNLIMITED never suspends the sender - it removes backpressure and turns a slow consumer into a memory leak.
CONFLATED and DROP_OLDEST silently drop values: correct only for a 'latest value wins' stream (a price ticker), wrong for an audit log.
A cancelled send may have already taken the element: onUndeliveredElement is how a resource is closed instead of leaked.
Never block a thread inside a coroutine on a channel; send/receive SUSPEND. Calling a blocking take() defeats the point.
